extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and students of dramatic theory (writers of tragedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and judging tragic drama in the classical sense: definitions, constituent parts, plot construction, character, diction, and performance-related elements. Focuses on producing a tragic effect (pity and fear) and the catharsis of those emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy is the imitation of an action that is serious and also, as having magnitude, complete in itself; in language with pleasurable accessories; in a dramatic, not in a narrative form; with incidents arousing pity and fear, wherewith to accomplish its catharsis of such emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies 'language with pleasurable accessories' as rhythm, harmony or song; some portions worked out in verse, others with song. Emphasizes imitation of action (not persons) and the aim to produce pity and fear leading to catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six formative parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: There are six parts of every tragedy: a Fable or Plot, Characters, Diction, Thought, Spectacle and Melody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the constituent elements from which tragedy is made; some are common with epic, some peculiar to tragedy. Use all where appropriate; nothing else besides these six.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the six parts, the Plot is the most important; Characters come second; Thought third; Diction fourth; Melody is a chief pleasurable accessory; Spectacle is the least artistic and has the least to do with the art of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if diction and character are excellent, a play without a strong Plot will fail to produce true tragic effect. Spectacle can enhance but should not substitute for the Plot's power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as primary—action, not persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is essentially an imitation of action and life; the Plot (combination of incidents) is the end and purpose of tragedy; characters are included for the sake of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet is chiefly a poet of Plots rather than of verses. One may have a play without strong Character but not without Plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action
rubrics_metrics.description: A story/Plot must represent one action, a complete whole, with its several incidents so closely connected that the transposal or withdrawal of any one of them will disjoin and dislocate the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity is not simply having one man as subject; avoid aggregating unrelated episodes even if they happen to the same person. Judge sameness/difference of tragedies primarily by their Complication and Denouement (i.e., Plot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must be complete with beginning, middle, and end
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole is that which has a beginning (not itself necessarily after anything), a middle (after one thing and before another), and an end (that which has nothing after it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-constructed Plot cannot begin or end arbitrarily; its beginning and end must be of the described forms. The Plot's magnitude should be enough to be taken in by memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate magnitude/length
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot must be of a length to be taken in by the memory; beauty requires a definite magnitude—neither too minute nor too vast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rough formula: a length that allows the hero to pass by a series of probable or necessary stages from misfortune to happiness, or from happiness to misfortune. Public-performance timing is external to poetic theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic plots
rubrics_metrics.description: An episodic Plot is one where there is neither probability nor necessity in the sequence of episodes and is the worst kind of simple Plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodes should be appropriate and derive from the Plot; stretching a Plot for players' sake often forces improbable episodes. Episodes in drama must be short and serve the Plot; long episodes belong to epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs. Complex Plots — Peripety and Discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are simple when the change in the hero's fortunes takes place without Peripety or Discovery, complex when they involve one or both. Peripety and Discovery are central parts of complex plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peripety and Discovery should arise from the structure of the Plot itself as necessary or probable consequences of antecedents. Complex plots (with these elements) are preferred for finest tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripety (Reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Peripety is the change from one state of things within the play to its opposite, produced by the probable or necessary sequence of events (e.g., Oedipus' case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Should arise naturally from preceding incidents; when combined with Discovery it most powerfully arouses pity and fear and helps produce the eventual ending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Discovery is a change from ignorance to knowledge (of persons or facts), leading to love or hate in personages marked for good or evil fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The finest Discoveries are those attended by Peripety and arising from the incidents themselves rather than from artifice. Discoveries may be of one party only or mutual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types and quality of Discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: Species of Discovery include: (1) by signs/marks; (2) poet's direct revelation; (3) through memory; (4) through reasoning; (5) composite from bad reasoning; (6) arising from the incidents themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ranked by artistry: (6) (incidents themselves) best; (3)–(4) good when natural; (1) and (2) less artistic—especially when they imply reflection or the poet forcing the revelation. Avoid low-artifice forms when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three Plot forms to avoid; ideal tragic protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid (1) a good man passing from happiness to misery; (2) a bad man passing from misery to happiness; (3) an extremely bad man falling from happiness into misery. Prefer an intermediate kind of personage whose misfortune is due to some error of judgment, not depravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pity is occasioned by undeserved misfortune; fear by that of one like ourselves. The perfect Plot has a single issue (not double) and the cause of fall lies in error rather than vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic incidents: source of pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents arousing pity and fear have greatest effect when they occur unexpectedly and as consequences of one another; family-deeds (murder within family) are especially piteous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poet should seek deeds of horror done within the family (brother on brother, son on father, mother on son, etc.). Best dramatic effect is produced by incidents that seem designed rather than mere chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffering as a component of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A third part of Plot is Suffering, defined as an action of a destructive or painful nature (murders, tortures, woundings, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suffering is one of the formative elements alongside Peripety and Discovery and must be integrated with the action to produce tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of Tragedy by quantity (structural divisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the point of view of separate sections, a tragedy has Prologue, Episode, Exode, and a choral portion distinguished into Parode and Stasimon; Commas and stage-songs appear in some plays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prologue = precedes the chorus's Parode; Episode = between whole choral songs; Exode = follows the last choral song; Parode = first statement of chorus; Stasimon = chorus song without anapaests/trochees; Commas = lamentation sung by chorus and actor together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complication and Denouement
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy is in part Complication (all up to the point just before the change in the hero's fortunes) and in part Denouement (from the beginning of the change to the end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both Complication and Denouement must be well mastered; many dramatists fail in Denouement after a good Complication. When comparing plays, assess sameness chiefly by their Complication and Denouement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as an actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors and an integral part of the whole, taking a share in the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the Chorus that shares in action (Sophocles) over later practice where songs are intercalary and unrelated to the Plot (Euripides, Agathon). Avoid songs that do not advance the Plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should: (1) be good (reveal a good moral purpose), (2) be appropriate (fit sex/status/role), (3) be like reality (lifelike), and (4) be consistent and the same throughout (even 'consistently inconsistent').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character actions and speech must be the probable or necessary outcome of their nature. Avoid incongruity and unbefitting behavior; inconsistency must be purposeful and consistently portrayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought and Diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the power of saying what is appropriate—what the personages say when proving a point or enunciating a truth; Diction is the composition of the verses (expression of thoughts in words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought belongs closely to rhetoric—speech should serve to prove/disprove, arouse emotion, or persuade. Diction should express the character's thought appropriately; do not confuse Thought with Character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody and Spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody is the greatest of the pleasurable accessories of Tragedy; Spectacle is the least artistic of all parts and more for costumier/stagecraft than the poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tragic effect is possible without performance; do not rely on Spectacle to supply essential tragic pleasure. Melody should be used as a pleasurable accessory that supports the imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic aim—probability and universals
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must describe a kind of thing that might happen—what is possible as being probable or necessary—rather than merely recount what has happened (history). Poetry makes universal statements about what such kinds of men will probably say or do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic truth is philosophical and general; poets may adapt historical material but should treat it so as to express the universal and probable. Do not rigidly adhere to tradition for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction method and craft guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing Plots and Diction, the poet should (1) put the actual scenes as far as possible before his eyes, (2) act his story with gestures where possible, and (3) simplify a story to a universal form before lengthening it with episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing and feeling the emotions aids convincing portrayal. Fix proper names only after the universal skeleton is worked out; ensure episodes are appropriate (e.g., fits of madness linked to plot), and avoid dramatizing entire epic bodies of incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four species of Tragedy and combining elements
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four distinct species of Tragedy: (1) complex (Peripety and Discovery), (2) tragedy of suffering, (3) tragedy of character, (4) spectacle-driven tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should aim to combine as many elements of interest as possible, or at least the most important among them, to produce the best tragic effect.
